claim: CAR-T therapy has produced unprecedented clinical outcomes for patients with hematologic malignancies.
source: Advances in chimeric antigen receptor modified T cell therapy (CAR-T) in recent years have shown enormous promise in cancer immunotherapy, which has produced unprecedented clinical outcomes, most notably for patients with hematologic malignancies (Singh et al., 2016; Park et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Singh et al., 2016 and Park et al., 2018

claim: CAR-T therapy is associated with severe toxicity and side effects including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity.
source: Despite the striking achievements, CAR-T therapy is also facing many challenges such as the treatment-related severe toxicity and side effects, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity (Hong et al., 2020; Freyer and Porter, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hong et al., 2020 and Freyer and Porter, 2020

claim: CRS is the most common acute toxicity associated with CAR-T therapy that causes fever, hypotension, and respiratory insufficiency.
source: CRS is the most common acute toxicity associated with an excessive immune response that causes fever, hypotension, and respiratory insufficiency.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about CRS symptoms

claim: CAR-T-induced neurotoxicity exhibits diverse neurologic symptoms such as tremors, expressive aphasia, and impaired attention.
source: The neurotoxicity induced by CAR-T therapy exhibits a diverse array of neurologic symptoms such as tremors, expressive aphasia, and impaired attention.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about neurotoxicity symptoms

claim: The precise mechanism that causes CAR-T-related life-threatening side effects remains unclear.
source: The precise mechanism that causes these life-threatening side effects remains unclear (Freyer and Porter, 2020; Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Freyer and Porter, 2020 and Jiang et al., 2019

claim: The success of CAR-T therapy in treating solid tumors is very limited.
source: On the other hand, the success of CAR-T therapy in treating solid tumors is still very limited (Martinez and Moon, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez and Moon, 2019

claim: The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) is one of the obstacles that diminishes the efficacy of CAR-T therapy, especially for solid tumors.
source: The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) is one of the obstacles that diminishes the efficacy of CAR-T therapy, especially for solid tumors.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about TME effects on CAR-T therapy

claim: The impact of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) on CAR-T therapy has been little studied.
source: Among the many factors that can modulate TME and immune response, the impact of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) on CAR-T therapy has been little studied.
evidence: Based on inference from the literature review presented

claim: MSC is a type of adult stem cell with high proliferative activity and multidirectional differentiation capacity.
source: MSC is a type of adult stem cell with high proliferative activity and multidirectional differentiation capacity.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about MSC characteristics

claim: MSCs have paracrine effects that are believed to underlie their therapeutic functions.
source: However, MSCs have additional paracrine effects that are believed to underlie their therapeutic functions (Jiang and Xu, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang and Xu, 2020

claim: MSCs can modulate extracellular matrix, promote angiogenesis, and suppress inflammation and apoptosis by secreting cytokines.
source: By secreting a variety of cytokines into the tissue microenvironment, it has been known that MSCs can modulate extracellular matrix, promote angiogenesis, and suppress inflammation and apoptosis (Keating, 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keating, 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2019

claim: MSC-secreted cytokines such as stromal cell-derived factor 1 and stem cell factor play important roles in hematopoietic and immune regulation.
source: Some MSC-secreted cytokines, such as stromal cell-derived factor 1 and stem cell factor, play important roles in hematopoietic and immune regulation (Kawaguchi et al., 2019; Markov et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawaguchi et al., 2019 and Markov et al., 2007

claim: MSCs can modulate the function of monocytic lineages cells, especially macrophages.
source: In addition, studies suggest that MSCs can modulate the function of monocytic lineages cells, especially macrophages (Németh et al., 2009; YlÖstalo et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Németh et al., 2009; YlÖstalo et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2011

claim: MSCs could directly affect the functionality and cellular responses of T cells, Tregs, and memory T cells.
source: Some reports also showed that MSCs could directly affect the functionality and cellular responses of T cells, Tregs, and memory T cells (Cen et al., 2019; Tumangelova-Yuzeir et al., 2019; Luque-Campos et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cen et al., 2019; Tumangelova-Yuzeir et al., 2019; Luque-Campos et al., 2019

claim: Human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) could be activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated macrophages to increase the expression and secretion of stanniocalcin-1 (STC1).
source: It was reported that human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) could be activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated macrophages to increase the expression and secretion of stanniocalcin-1 (STC1) (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oh et al., 2014

claim: STC1 was originally identified as a calcium/phosphate regulating hormone in bony fishes.
source: STC1 was a mitochondria-related glycoprotein originally identified as a calcium/phosphate regulating hormone in bony fishes, and later on, it was found to be a pleiotropic factor involved in various degenerative diseases such as ocular and renal disease, as well as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Yeung et al., 2012; Ohkouchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yeung et al., 2012 and Ohkouchi et al., 2015

claim: STC1 is a pleiotropic factor involved in various degenerative diseases such as ocular and renal disease, as well as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
source: STC1 was a mitochondria-related glycoprotein originally identified as a calcium/phosphate regulating hormone in bony fishes, and later on, it was found to be a pleiotropic factor involved in various degenerative diseases such as ocular and renal disease, as well as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Yeung et al., 2012; Ohkouchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yeung et al., 2012 and Ohkouchi et al., 2015

claim: STC1 could improve the cell survival and regeneration of MSCs in a paracrine fashion.
source: STC1 could improve the cell survival and regeneration of MSCs in a paracrine fashion (Ono et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ono et al., 2015

claim: STC1 played an oncogenic role in various types of tumors.
source: There was also evidence suggesting that STC1 played an oncogenic role in various types of tumors (Du et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2010

claim: High STC1 expression is associated with the poor clinical outcome of breast cancer.
source: Based on a retrospective study of ~1500 clinical samples, it was concluded that high STC1 expression is associated with the poor clinical outcome of breast cancer (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2015

claim: STC1 is involved in several oxidative and cancer-related signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun NH(2)-terminal kinase (JNK) pathways.
source: It was proved that STC1 is involved in several oxidative and cancer-related signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun NH(2)-terminal kinase (JNK) pathways (Nguyen et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2009 and Chan et al., 2017

claim: The expression and secretion of STC1 in cancer tissue can be stimulated by external stimuli, including external cytokines and oxidative stress.
source: The expression and secretion of STC1 in cancer tissue can be stimulated by external stimuli, including external cytokines and oxidative stress (Nguyen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2009

claim: Under hypoxia conditions, STC1 could be modulated by Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) to facilitate the reprogramming of tumor metabolism from oxidative to glycolytic metabolism.
source: Under hypoxia conditions, STC1 could be modulated by Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) to facilitate the reprogramming of tumor metabolism from oxidative to glycolytic metabolism (Yeung et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeung et al., 2005

claim: STC1 was reported to participate in the process of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, which is associated with tumor invasion and the reshape of the tumor microenvironment, as well as increasing therapy resistance.
source: STC1 was also reported to participate in the process of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, which is associated with tumor invasion and the reshape of the tumor microenvironment, as well as increasing therapy resistance (Pastushenko and Blanpain, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastushenko and Blanpain, 2019

claim: Stable knockdown of STC1 in hMSC inhibited cell migration.
source: To investigate whether knockdown of STC1 affects cell migration, wound healing and transwell chamber assays were performed. After creating a 'scratch' in a monolayer of hMSCs, the closure of the gap was determined after 24 hr. As shown in Figure 1D, compared to control hMSCs, the gap was less filled in hMSCshSTC1. The inhibitory effect on cell migration was further confirmed by a transwell assay. As shown in Figure 1E, there were significant migration and invasion observed in hMSCsshCtrl, whereas there was a >30% reduction in migration across the transwell chamber membrane in hMSCsshSTC1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from wound healing and transwell assays shown in Figure 1D and 1E

claim: Stable knockdown of STC1 in hMSC slightly suppressed cell proliferation.
source: STC1 stable knockdown in hMSCs exhibited a minor effect in cell survival (Figure 1B) and slightly reduced proliferation rate based on the small increase in the proportion of cells in G0/G1 phases versus that in the S phase (Figure 1C) as determined by MTT (3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl]-2,5 diphenyl tetrazolium bromide) and Fluorescence-activated Cell Sorting (FACS) analysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from MTT and FACS analysis shown in Figure 1B and 1C

claim: Knockdown of STC1 did not cause apoptosis of hMSCs.
source: To further determine whether knockdown of STC1 may have any lethal effect, apoptosis was determined by two different assays. To measure the early apoptosis, cells were stained with the Alexa Fluor 488 annexin V and the propidium iodide (PI) followed by flow cytometry to detect apoptosis-associated phosphatidylserine (PS) expression and membrane permeability (Figure 1F). Parallelly, no DNA fragmentation was detected as determined with the TUNEL assay (Figure 1G, the green dots were from the background due to overexposure). Both studies showed that knockdown of STC1 did not cause apoptosis of hMSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from annexin V/PI staining and TUNEL assay shown in Figure 1F and 1G

claim: The presence of hMSCs inhibited CAR-T cell killing activity toward Pfeiffer cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, 67% of Pfeiffer cells were killed after being exposed to CAR-T cells for 24 hr, and 93% were killed at 48 hr as compared to mock-treated control. After adding hMSCs into the co-culture, the cell-killing activity of CAR-T was significantly inhibited (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LDH cytotoxicity assay shown in Figure 2A

claim: Knockdown of STC1 in hMSCs completely abrogated the inhibition of CAR-T cytotoxicity by hMSCs.
source: Interestingly, the inhibitory effect of hMSCs on CAR-T cytotoxicity could be completely abrogated if knockdown STC1 gene in hMSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LDH cytotoxicity assay shown in Figure 2A

claim: Co-culturing with hMSCs caused an increase of CD4+ T cells and a decrease of CD8+ T cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2B and C, the ratio between CD4+ and CD8+ was about 1:4 when there were no hMSCs in co-culture (Figure 2C). However, the addition of hMSC caused a significant increase of CD4+ and a decrease of CD8+ T cells (Figure 2B), resulting in a ratio change to 2:1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: Co-culturing with hMSCs caused an increase of Treg cells.
source: Similar to the change of CD4+ T cells, the percentage of regulatory T cells (Treg) was also significantly increased from ~3 to 12% when co-culture with hMSC (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 2D and 2E

claim: Using hMSCshSTC1, all the changes in T cell subsets were completely reversed back to the level similar to that of co-culture without hMSCs.
source: When using hMSCshSTC1, all the changes were completely reversed back to the level similar to that of co-culture without hMSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 2B-E

claim: CD8+ T cells are directly responsible for specific lytic activity against lymphoma.
source: This explains the reduced CAR-T cytotoxicity since CD8+ T cells are directly responsible for specific lytic activity against lymphoma (Sommermeyer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommermeyer et al., 2016

claim: Tregs account for 5–10% of the total number of CD4+ T cells and play a role in suppressing the function of T cells and other immune cells.
source: Tregs, which account for 5–10% of the total number of CD4+ T cells, are known to play a role in suppressing the function of T cells and other immune cells (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: The addition of hMSC to the cell co-culture stimulated the expression of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) and programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1).
source: As shown in Figure 2F, the addition of hMSC to the cell co-culture stimulated the expression of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) and programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 2F

claim: IDO is an intracellular enzyme that converts tryptophan into inhibitory metabolites for T-cell activity.
source: IDO is an intracellular enzyme that converts tryptophan into inhibitory metabolites for T-cell activity (Ninomiya et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ninomiya et al., 2015

claim: PD-L1 is expressed in tumor cells and immune cells contributing to the immune-suppressive TME.
source: PD-L1 is expressed in tumor cells and immune cells contributing to the immune-suppressive TME (Ribas and Hu-Lieskovan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribas and Hu-Lieskovan, 2016

claim: When using hMSCshSTC1, the expression level of IDO and PD-L1 was both significantly reduced by more than 50%.
source: When using hMSCshSTC1, the expression level of IDO and PD-L1 was both significantly reduced by more than 50%, though still higher than that without hMSC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 2F

claim: Macrophages could activate hMSCs to secrete STC1.
source: In the co-culture model, M2 macrophages were included since a previous study showed that macrophages could activate hMSCs to secrete STC1 (Cen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cen et al., 2019

claim: The macrophage is a critical part of immune response and an important regulator of immunotherapy.
source: In addition, the macrophage is a critical part of immune response and an important regulator of immunotherapy (DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome is a critical component of the innate immune system mediating caspase-1 activation and proinflammatory cytokines secretion in response to harmful stimuli.
source: The NLRP3 inflammasome is a critical component of the innate immune system mediating caspase-1 activation and proinflammatory cytokines secretion in response to harmful stimuli such as infection and endogenous stress (Menu and Vince, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Menu and Vince, 2011

claim: The release of cleaved caspase-1 p20 was detected after the PMA polarization of THP-1 cells to form the M1 macrophages.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the release of cleaved caspase-1 p20 in cell lysates, which is the indicator of caspase-1 activation, was detected after the PMA polarization of THP-1 cells to form the M1 macrophages (M-THP1).

claim: Following co-culture with CD19 CAR-T, the level of cleaved caspase-1 was significantly upregulated.
source: Following co-culture with CD19 CAR-T, the level of cleaved caspase-1 was significantly upregulated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 3A

claim: The increase of active caspase-1 was abrogated when hMSCs were added into the co-culture.
source: The increase of active caspase-1 was abrogated when hMSCs were added into the co-culture.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 3A

claim: Knockdown of STC1 led to another reverse and completely blocked the inhibitory function of hMSCs on active caspase-1.
source: knock-down of STC1 led to another reverse and completely blocked the inhibitory function of hMSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 3A

claim: The cleaved IL-1β mature form and absent-in-melanoma 2 (AIM2) are two key components of the inflammasome.
source: Concomitant with the reduction in active caspase-1, the cleaved IL-1β mature form and absent-in-melanoma 2 (AIM2), two key components of the inflammasome (Kelley et al., 2019), were both increasingly expressed following M-THP1 polarization and further incubation with CAR-T (Figure 3A).

claim: The addition of hMSC in the cell co-culture showed a strong inhibition of IL-1β and AIM2, and their expression level was returned to the base level of Pfeiffer plus CAR-T.

claim: The immune-suppressive effect of hMSC was through its impact on macrophages, not CAR-T or Pfeiffer cells.
source: This result suggests that the immune-suppressive effect of hMSC was through its impact on macrophages, not CAR-T or Pfeiffer cells.

claim: Knockdown of STC1 abrogated the inhibition of hMSC on IL-1β and AIM2.
source: Knockdown of STC1 abrogated the inhibition of hMSC on IL-1β and AIM2 (Figure 3A).

claim: The levels of IL-1β in the supernatants measured by ELISA showed similar results as cell lysate.

claim: Exogenous STC1 is internalized by macrophages within 10 min and localizes to mitochondria to suppress superoxide generation.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the major stimuli that activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, and it was reported that exogenous STC1 is internalized by macrophages within 10 min and localizes to mitochondria to suppress superoxide generation (Wang et al., 2009).

claim: The presence of hMSCsshCtrl markedly suppressed both the cellular and mitochondrial ROS induced by the co-culture of CAR-T cells, tumor cells, and macrophages.

claim: hMSCs inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages by inhibiting the oxidative burst.

source: As shown in Figure 4A, CD19 CAR-T treatment combined with the injection of hMSCshSTC1 achieved a significant curative effect, and the tumors nearly disappeared at day 38.

claim: The number of IL-1β positive cells ranged from 76 to 100% in the hMSCshSTC1 group, while it ranged from 5 to 20% in the hMSCshCtrl group in tumor tissue on day 10.
source: Based on the immunohistochemical analysis of IL-1β in tumor tissue on day 10, the number of positive cells (brownish-yellow staining) ranged from 76 to 100% in the hMSCshSTC1 group, while it ranged from 5 to 20% in the hMSCshCtrl group, indicating that hMSC could suppress TME and STC1 knockdown significantly diminished this impact (Figure 4B).

claim: A large amount of CD4+ T cells were detected in the hMSCshCtrl group but much less in the hMSCshSTC1 group in tumor tissue.

claim: The amount of CD8+ T cells was significantly increased in the hMSCshSTC1 group compared to that of the hMSCshCtrl group in tumor tissue.

claim: The amount of Treg cells was evidently increased in the hMSCshCtrl group compared to that of the hMSCshSTC1 group in tumor tissue.

evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4B

claim: Mice in CAR-T combined with the hMSCshSTC1 group had the longest survival with no death by day 38.
source: The survival time of mice demonstrated that mice in CAR-T combined with the hMSCshSTC1 group had the longest survival with no death by day 38 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from survival analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: Compared to the control group with no CAR-T treatment, tumor spreading in the hMSCshCtrl group was slower, and all survived for 6 days more.
source: Compared to the control group with no CAR-T treatment, tumor spreading in the hMSCshCtrl group was slower, and all survived for 6 days more.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from survival analysis shown in Figure 4D
